newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. Q3 GDP growth 2.0 percent.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. Q3 GDP growth 2.0 percent.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Commerce Department reported that third quarter U.S. Gross Domestic Product grew at a revised 2.0 percent pace against a preliminary reading of 2.2 percent for the third quarter. Experts had expected revised third quarter GDP growth of 1.7 percent.
LARRY CHIMERINE, CHIEF ECONOMIST, ECONOMIC STRATEGY INSTITUTE: "This is slightly higher (than Wall Street estimates) but it really doesn't change the assessment of what's happening in the economy."
ASTRID ADOLFSON, SENIOR ECONOMIST, MCM MONEYWATCH INC:
"It's a slight upward revision to final sales and downward to inventories, so they don't change the picture much."

Commenting on whether the revision in inventories might suggest a fourth-quarter pickup in manufacturing, Adolfson said: "It might, but it's so small it's not worth comment. It's pretty much in line with expectations."

JOSEPH CARSON, CHIEF FIXED INCOME ECONOMIST, DEUTSCHE MORGAN GRENFELL: "The number came in according to script -- a little less inventories and more final demand. I don't think it changes the picture for the current quarter. The inventory overhang is still there but not as much as estimated.
"The mix in the fourth quarter will be different (than the third quarter), with more final demand growth and less inventory accumulation."
MARTIN MAURO, SENIOR ECONOMIST AT MERRILL LYNCH: "I would call this close to a non-event...There were really no surprises.
"Very little revisions: the net export deficit was revised wider, which is what we thought, but not much in the way of revisions to consumer spending or investment.
"We're still looking for fourth quarter GDP to be close to 4.0 percent. This doesn't really change that.
"The real question for the fourth quarter is what are consumers going to do after the lackluster third quarter."

DAN SETO, SENIOR ECONOMIST, THE NIKKO SECURITIES CO INTERNATIONAL INC: "GDP is revised down but not as much as anticipated. The trade gap was obviously the story, as well as inventories -- they subtracted more from GDP or contributed less, in the case of (business) inventories."

"Final sales are actually a little stronger, now up 0.4 percent versus 0.3 percent ... it doesn't change the picture a whole lot. It's not something we can make a lot out of, but it is surprising we did not get (GDP) below 2.0 percent."
NEAL SOSS, SENIOR ECONOMIC ADVISOR, C.S. FIRST BOSTON:

"The number is broadly consistent with the pattern we thought was in place for the third quarter. Consumption was soft, although it has been revised up a tad. It still shows that the consumer, for whatever reason, stopped having animal spirits as we went into the summer."
He added, "A very large fraction of GDP was from inventories. We saw the trade side weakening, and that is because the economies of our economic partners are still soft."
